title: Which joins can broadcast
prompt: Join `shipments` to `warehouses` on `warehouse_id` four ways: inner, left, right and full. Write `solve(shipments, warehouses)` so it returns one row per join type with `how`, `rows` and `broadcast`.
rules: Keep `shipments` on the left and `warehouses` on the right in every join. Put `F.broadcast` on a side Spark can broadcast for that join type, whenever there is one.
`rows` is the number of rows the join returns. `broadcast` is whether its plan uses a broadcast hash join: use `uses_broadcast` from the starter.
The starter turns automatic broadcasting and adaptive execution off, so only your hints count. Return the columns `how`, `rows`, `broadcast`.
hints: The side whose every row is kept has to be streamed past the lookup table, so it can't be the broadcast one.
Inner keeps neither side whole, left keeps the left side, right the right side. A full join keeps both.
Collect `(how, joined.count(), uses_broadcast(joined))` tuples in a list and pass it to the `spark.createDataFrame` line. A missing key never matches, so outer joins keep those rows unmatched.
explanation: An inner join can broadcast either side. A left join keeps every shipment, so only `warehouses` can be broadcast; a right join keeps every warehouse, so the hint goes on `shipments`: `F.broadcast(shipments).join(warehouses, "warehouse_id", "right")`. A full join keeps both sides, so no hint can be used and Spark quietly runs a sort-merge join. That gives `True, True, True, False` on any data. The row counts are ordinary join semantics: missing warehouse ids never match, so they come back unmatched in the outer joins, and a warehouse listed twice doubles its shipments. The hints never change the counts. Swapping the tables to broadcast `warehouses` in the right join turns it into a different join, which keeps shipments instead of warehouses.
